etymology: From Middle English chappen (to crack, to split), related to chop; the archaic past participle appearing once in the Authorized Version, in Jeremiah's description of drought during the reign of the last kings of Judah.
biblical_def:
Because the ground is chapt, for there was no rain in the earth.

Chapt appears once in the Authorized Version, in Jeremiah's account of a severe drought, the ground cracked and split from lack of moisture, described so that the plowmen were ashamed, they covered their heads (Jer 14:4) — farmers so helpless before the barren, unworkable soil that they hid their faces in shame at their own uselessness. The chapter that follows is a lament woven through with confession, Jeremiah pleading for Judah though he knows the nation's own iniquities have brought the judgment: our backslidings are many; we have sinned against thee (Jer 14:7). The drought is not treated as mere meteorology but as covenant discipline, consistent with the warnings given through Moses centuries earlier that disobedience would bring a land where the heaven that is over thy head shall be brass, and the earth that is under thee shall be iron (Deu 28:23). Even the wild creatures suffer alongside the people — the hind also calved in the field, and forsook it, because there was no grass (Jer 14:5) — a reminder that covenant unfaithfulness has consequences reaching beyond the guilty into the whole created order under their care, a pattern Paul later names when he writes that the creature itself also shall be delivered from the bondage of corruption (Rom 8:21), waiting for a redemption sin itself first broke.

webster_full: CHAP, v.i. To crack; to open in long slits, as the ground or the skin.
CHAPT, adj. Archaic past participle: cracked, split open, as parched ground.

corruption_summary: A purely naturalistic reading of drought as weather alone misses Jeremiah's own theological frame, which reads such disasters as covenant discipline calling the nation to confession rather than mere misfortune to be weathered.
corruption_paragraphs: Modern instinct explains drought entirely by meteorology and climate, a true but incomplete account when Scripture's own prophets consistently read such events as covenant signals calling a nation to self-examination and repentance, not merely to endurance.

This entry faces no significant postmodern redefinition. The principle to recover is Jeremiah's own response: not denial, not mere resignation, but confession — 'we have sinned against thee' (Jer 14:7) — the response the chapt ground was meant to provoke.

etymology: From Old French chargier (to load, to burden, to command), from Latin carricare; the archaic second-person singular past tense ("thou chargedst") appearing once in the Authorized Version, in Moses' recollection of the giving of the law at Sinai.
biblical_def:
For thou chargedst us, saying, Set bounds about the mount, and sanctify it.

Chargedst appears once in the Authorized Version, in Moses' words to the LORD at Sinai, recalling the specific command God had given: set bounds about the mount, and sanctify it (Exo 19:23), a boundary marking the mountain as too holy for the people to approach on pain of death, as the LORD had already warned whosoever toucheth the mount shall be surely put to death (Exo 19:12). The exchange in Exodus 19 shows Moses actively engaging with God's instructions, going up and down the mountain repeatedly to relay warnings and receive clarifications, careful that the people not break through unto the LORD to gaze, and many of them perish (Exo 19:21). The bounded mountain, smoking, quaking, and thundering as the LORD descended upon it in fire, stands as one of Scripture's most vivid pictures of the terror proper to an unmediated approach to a holy God under the law, a terror the author of Hebrews later contrasts directly with the access believers now have: ye are not come unto the mount that might be touched, and that burned with fire... but ye are come unto mount Sion (Heb 12:18, 22). The bounds Moses was charged to set were themselves a mercy, protecting a sinful people from a holiness they could not otherwise survive approaching.

corruption_summary: A casual approach to God that treats access to Him as automatic and without cost misses what the bounded mountain teaches about the holiness sin makes dangerous to approach apart from a mediator.
corruption_paragraphs: A therapeutic religious culture that assumes God is simply, always approachable without qualification can lose the weight this scene carries: even Moses, God's own chosen mediator, had to relay careful bounds to protect the people from a holiness that would otherwise have consumed them.

This entry faces no significant postmodern redefinition. The principle to recover is Hebrews' own comparison: the terror of Sinai's bounded mountain has been replaced, not by casualness, but by the far greater access purchased through Christ's blood, which speaketh better things than that of Abel (Heb 12:24).

etymology: From Old French charmer (to enchant, to sing a charm over), from Latin carmen (song, incantation); the past tense appearing once in the Authorized Version, in Jeremiah's warning of coming judgment upon Judah.
biblical_def:
I will send serpents, cockatrices, among you, which will not be charmed, and they shall bite you.

Charmed appears once in the Authorized Version, in Jeremiah's oracle of judgment, describing venomous serpents the LORD would send against Judah, creatures which will not be charmed — immune to the snake-charmer's usual art of subduing or pacifying dangerous serpents through sound or skill. The image draws its force from the ancient practice of serpent-charming, a real skill Scripture elsewhere acknowledges (Psa 58:4-5, Ecc 10:11), and inverts it into a picture of judgment no human skill can avert: these serpents will bite regardless of whatever charm is attempted against them. The threat belongs to a series of judgments in Jeremiah 8 following the nation's persistent refusal to repent, described in the chapter's own indictment: no man repented him of his wickedness, saying, What have I done? (Jer 8:6). The uncharmable serpents picture judgment that has passed beyond the point where any human remedy, technique, or clever mitigation can turn it aside — a sobering warning that a people who persistently refuse the ordinary means of repentance may eventually face a judgment for which no charm, political, religious, or otherwise, remains effective.

webster_full: CHARM, v.t. To subdue or control by song, incantation, or magical art.
CHARMED, v. Past tense: subdued or controlled by such art; here negated — unable to be so controlled.

corruption_paragraphs: Modern problem-solving instincts can assume every crisis has a technical or strategic fix waiting to be found; Jeremiah's image specifically denies this for the judgment he describes, a sobering counter to unlimited confidence in human ingenuity.

This entry faces no significant postmodern redefinition. The principle to recover is Jeremiah's own diagnosis of the real problem: not a lack of clever remedies but 'no man repented him of his wickedness' (Jer 8:6) — the only remedy Scripture actually offers is repentance, not a better charm.

etymology: From Old French charmer (to enchant), from Latin carmen (song, incantation); the present participle appearing once in the Authorized Version, in the Psalmist's description of the wicked's stubborn refusal to hear correction.
biblical_def:
Which will not hearken to the voice of charmers, charming never so wisely.

Charming appears once in the Authorized Version, in Psalm 58, David's indictment of unjust judges, described first as deaf adders that stoppeth her ear; which will not hearken to the voice of charmers, charming never so wisely (Psa 58:4-5). The image draws on the ancient practice of serpent-charming, here applied with pointed irony: however skillfully, however wisely the charmer performs his craft, the deaf adder simply will not hear, its own deafness rendering the charmer's genuine skill useless. David's target is not literal serpents but human judges who wrest judgment... in the earth (Psa 58:2), men so hardened in injustice that no wisdom offered to them, however sound, penetrates their willful deafness. The psalm's severity — break their teeth, O God, in their mouth (Psa 58:6) — is imprecatory prayer against entrenched, institutionalized wickedness, asking God to do what human wisdom, however wisely charming, has failed to accomplish. The psalm ends not in despair but in confidence that a righteous verdict will finally stand: verily he is a God that judgeth in the earth (Psa 58:11), a reminder that when human courts fail the deaf-adder test, the ultimate court has not.

CHARMING, v. Present participle: performing the act of charming, here applied ironically.

corruption_paragraphs: Modern persuasion culture can assume the right technique or messaging will eventually move any resistant party; David's deaf-adder image specifically denies this for entrenched, willful injustice, a sober counter to unlimited confidence in rhetoric or strategy alone.

This entry faces no significant postmodern redefinition. The principle to recover is the psalm's own resolution: where human wisdom, however charming, fails to move hardened injustice, the answer is not despair but prayer to the God 'that judgeth in the earth' (Psa 58:11).

etymology: From Old French eschec (a check, as in chess), from Persian shah (king); appearing once in the Authorized Version as a noun, in Job's response to Zophar's harsh accusation.
biblical_def:
I have heard the check of my reproach, and the spirit of my understanding causeth me to answer.

Check appears once in the Authorized Version as a noun meaning a rebuke or reprimand, in Job's opening words responding to Zophar's first speech, which had accused Job of lies and mockery and insisted that God exacteth of thee less than thine iniquity deserveth (Job 11:6). Job names what he has just heard plainly — a check, a reproach, a rebuke aimed at correcting him — and states that his understanding compels him to answer it, not to let the accusation stand unaddressed. What follows in Job 12-14 is among the most theologically dense material in the book, Job affirming God's incomparable wisdom and power (Job 12:13) even while insisting, against his friends' simplistic formula, that his own suffering is not proof of hidden, proportionate sin. Job's willingness to answer the check rather than either capitulate to false accusation or refuse to engage at all models something the book commends throughout: honest wrestling with hard words, tested against Scripture's own standard, rather than either silent submission to error or prideful refusal to hear correction that might, in fact, be just. The book's own conclusion vindicates Job's basic integrity even while rebuking elements of his speech, a complexity later chapters resolve without ever validating his friends' original, false diagnosis.

CHECK, n. A stop; restraint; control upon action or speech.

corruption_summary: A passive religious temperament that treats any correction as automatically to be received in silence, or an opposite pride that refuses all correction outright, both miss the balanced model Job displays of testing a rebuke honestly before God rather than reacting by either extreme.
corruption_paragraphs: Some pious instincts equate humility with never answering a rebuke, while an opposite instinct treats any pushback as automatically prideful; Job does neither, hearing the check honestly and then answering it with reasoned, Scripture-grounded argument.

This entry faces no significant postmodern redefinition. The principle to recover is Job's own balance: a rebuke deserves a real hearing and, where it is false, a real answer, neither silenced by false humility nor dismissed by pride, tested finally by whether it accords with the truth about God.

etymology: From Old French eschequier (chessboard), from eschec (check); appearing once in the Authorized Version, describing the ornamental network decorating the pillars of Solomon's temple.
biblical_def:
And nets of checker work, and wreaths of chain work, for the chapiters.

Checker appears once in the Authorized Version, describing the decorative latticework, nets of checker work, cast in bronze by Hiram of Tyre for the two great pillars, Jachin and Boaz, standing at the porch of Solomon's temple (1Ki 7:15-22). The pattern of interwoven, crossed lines — the same visual idea preserved in the modern word checkered — combined with wreaths of chain work and pomegranates to form an elaborate crown atop each pillar, seven for the one chapiter, and seven for the other. The extraordinary craftsmanship lavished on these two pillars, which supported no roof and bore no structural weight, illustrates a principle running through the whole temple account: beauty and skill devoted to God's house as an act of worship in itself, not merely function dressed up afterward. Hiram, described as filled with wisdom, and understanding, and cunning to work all works in brass (1Ki 7:14), stands in a line with Bezaleel at the tabernacle centuries earlier, another craftsman explicitly filled with the spirit of God, in wisdom, and in understanding, and in knowledge, and in all manner of workmanship (Exo 31:3) — Scripture's consistent testimony that artistic skill itself is a gift of God, properly exercised in His service.

webster_full: CHECKER, n. A pattern of crossing lines forming alternating squares.
CHECKER WORK, n. Decorative work in this crossed, latticed pattern.
In 1 Kings 7:17 the word describes bronze latticework crowning the temple pillars Jachin and Boaz.

corruption_summary: A narrowly utilitarian view of worship, treating only explicitly verbal or doctrinal elements as spiritually significant, misses Scripture's own testimony that skilled craftsmanship and beauty, offered to God, are themselves an act of worship, not merely decoration added afterward.
corruption_paragraphs: A pragmatic instinct can treat ornamentation as unnecessary excess compared to more obviously spiritual concerns; the temple account instead spends extensive space describing craftsmanship precisely because Scripture takes beauty offered to God seriously as worship, not indulgence.

This entry faces no significant postmodern redefinition. The principle to recover is the pattern set by Bezaleel at the tabernacle and Hiram at the temple alike: artistic skill is itself a gift of the Spirit of God, and its careful exercise in His house honors Him as truly as any spoken word.

etymology: From Old French chiere (face, countenance) with the suffix -ful and -ness; appearing once in the Authorized Version, in Paul's instruction on spiritual gifts exercised for the body of Christ.
biblical_def:
He that sheweth mercy, with cheerfulness.

Cheerfulness appears once in the Authorized Version, closing Paul's list of gifts in Romans 12: prophecy, ministry, teaching, exhortation, giving, ruling, and finally he that sheweth mercy, with cheerfulness (Rom 12:6-8). Paul's concern throughout the passage is not merely that gifts be exercised but that each be exercised in the manner fitting its nature — giving with simplicity, ruling with diligence, and mercy with cheerfulness, because mercy shown grudgingly, however technically performed, fails to embody the very thing it claims to give. The instruction anticipates Paul's own later teaching to the Corinthians that every man according as he purposeth in his heart, so let him give; not grudgingly, or of necessity: for God loveth a cheerful giver (2Co 9:7), applying the same principle across the whole range of Christian service rather than to financial giving alone. The verse sits within Paul's larger argument in Romans 12 that believers, having received mercy themselves (Rom 12:1), form one body with many members, each gift a grace given, not earned, and each therefore to be exercised as an overflow of that received mercy rather than as a burdensome duty performed for appearance or obligation.

webster_full: CHEER, n. Gaiety; animation; a state of gladness.
CHEERFULNESS, n. A habitual state of good spirits; freedom from gloom or reluctance.

corruption_summary: A works-focused religious culture can treat correct outward action as sufficient regardless of the heart's disposition, missing Paul's insistence that mercy shown without cheerfulness fails to embody the mercy it claims to offer.
corruption_paragraphs: A checklist approach to Christian service can measure faithfulness only by whether an act was performed, not by the spirit in which it was done; Paul specifically names the manner of each gift's exercise as part of its proper obedience, not an optional extra.

This entry faces no significant postmodern redefinition. The principle to recover is Paul's own consistent teaching: God's grace received freely produces grace given freely, and mercy shown with cheerfulness, not obligation, is the mark of a gift genuinely flowing from mercy already known.

etymology: From Old English cyrin (churn, vessel for making butter); appearing once in the Authorized Version, in Proverbs' warning against provoking strife through anger.
biblical_def:
Surely the churning of milk bringeth forth butter, and the wringing of the nose bringeth forth blood.

Churning appears once in the Authorized Version, in Proverbs' closing chapter of practical wisdom, in a proverb built from two everyday, agricultural observations to illustrate a third, moral one: surely the churning of milk bringeth forth butter, and the wringing of the nose bringeth forth blood: so the forcing of wrath bringeth forth strife (Pro 30:33). The logic is one of cause and inevitable effect — churn milk long and vigorously enough, and butter results; twist a nose hard enough, and blood results; provoke and force anger deliberately, and strife results, as surely and as naturally as the first two everyday processes. The proverb belongs to the sayings of Agur, a wisdom collection notable for its intensely concrete, physical illustrations drawn from ordinary rural life — ants, conies, locusts, spiders, the way of an eagle in the air (Pro 30:24-31) — teaching abstract moral truth through observation of a world its author saw as a coherent, God-ordered system where causes reliably produce their proper effects. The proverb functions as a warning rather than an endorsement: just as no wise man deliberately wrings a nose to make it bleed, no wise man deliberately forces or provokes wrath, knowing full well what it will produce.
webster_summary: Webster (1828), from CHURN: to agitate milk or cream to produce butter; here as a household analogy for the inevitable result of provoked, forced wrath.
webster_full: CHURN, v.t. To agitate cream or milk in a vessel to separate the butter.
CHURNING, n. The act or process of churning; producing butter by agitation.
In Proverbs 30:33 the word forms an analogy: churned milk yields butter as surely as forced wrath yields strife.

scriptures: Surely the churning of milk bringeth forth butter, and the wringing of the nose bringeth forth blood: so the forcing of wrath bringeth forth strife.
corruption_summary: A culture that treats venting or provoking anger as harmless emotional release misses Proverbs' plain causal claim, that forced wrath produces strife as reliably and predictably as any physical process produces its natural effect.
corruption_paragraphs: Popular wisdom can treat expressing anger freely as always healthy catharsis; Proverbs' analogy insists instead that deliberately forced or provoked wrath has a predictable, near-mechanical result, and that result is strife, not release.

This entry faces no significant postmodern redefinition. The principle to recover is Proverbs' own consistent counsel elsewhere: he that is slow to wrath is of great understanding (Pro 14:29), and the wise man's task is to avoid the churning that produces strife, not to master the art of provoking it skillfully.

etymology: From Old French cler, from Latin clarus (bright, clear); the comparative form appearing once in the Authorized Version, in Zophar's promise to Job of restoration following repentance.
biblical_def:
Thine age shall be clearer than the noonday; thou shalt shine forth, thou shalt be as the morning.

Clearer appears once in the Authorized Version, in Zophar's first speech to Job, promising that if Job would but put away iniquity, thine age shall be clearer than the noonday, a picture of bright, unclouded restoration following genuine repentance (Job 11:13-17). The promise itself, considered as general wisdom, echoes true biblical patterns elsewhere — the path of the just is as the shining light, that shineth more and more unto the perfect day (Pro 4:18) — but Zophar's application to Job's specific case is the very thing the book as a whole exposes as false counsel, since Job's suffering was not, as his friends insisted, proportionate punishment for hidden sin requiring this kind of repentance-and-restoration formula. God's later verdict on Zophar and the other two friends is severe: my wrath is kindled against thee, and against thy two friends: for ye have not spoken of me the thing that is right, as my servant Job hath (Job 42:7). The image of a life growing clearer than the noonday remains a true picture of restoration in its proper place, but Job teaches that not every season of darkness is a hidden sin awaiting confession, and a comforter's task is not always to prescribe the formula that worked in a different situation.
webster_summary: Webster (1828), from CLEAR: bright; free from clouds or obscurity; the comparative form here of Zophar's promised restoration to Job, true doctrine wrongly applied.
webster_full: CLEAR, adj. Bright; free from clouds, mist, or obscurity.
CLEARER, adj. The comparative degree: brighter or more unclouded than another thing compared.
In Job 11:17 the word promises restoration 'clearer than the noonday' following repentance.
The image echoes true wisdom elsewhere: 'the path of the just... shineth more and more' (Pro 4:18).
God later rebukes Zophar's application of this true principle to Job's specific, undeserved suffering (Job 42:7).
scriptures: And thine age shall be clearer than the noonday; thou shalt shine forth, thou shalt be as the morning.
corruption_summary: A rigid retribution theology that assumes every suffering must be traceable to specific hidden sin repeats exactly Zophar's error, using a true principle of restoration to wrongly diagnose a case Scripture itself says was not what the principle addressed.
corruption_paragraphs: Well-meaning comforters can reach for a true biblical promise and misapply it as a universal formula, precisely Zophar's error: the promise of restoration after repentance is sound doctrine, but its application here assumed a cause for Job's suffering the book explicitly denies.

This entry faces no significant postmodern redefinition. The principle to recover is the book of Job's own hard lesson: true doctrine, wrongly applied to a suffering person's particular case, becomes the very thing God rebukes as not speaking 'the thing that is right' (Job 42:7).

etymology: From Old French cler, from Latin clarus (bright, clear), with the abstract suffix -ness; appearing once in the Authorized Version, in Exodus's account of the elders of Israel seeing the God of Israel at Sinai.
biblical_def:
As it were a paved work of a sapphire stone, and as it were the body of heaven in his clearness.

Clearness appears once in the Authorized Version, in Exodus's astonishing account of Moses, Aaron, Nadab, Abihu, and seventy elders of Israel ascending the mountain and seeing the God of Israel, described only by the pavement beneath what they beheld: as it were a paved work of a sapphire stone, and as it were the body of heaven in his clearness (Exo 24:9-10). The text is remarkably restrained, describing not God's form but only the transparent, brilliant clarity of what lay under His feet, consistent with Scripture's careful reluctance elsewhere to describe the invisible God in visual terms that could invite idolatry. What follows the vision is equally striking: upon the nobles of the children of Israel he laid not his hand: also they saw God, and did eat and drink (Exo 24:11), an act of covenant fellowship, a meal in God's own presence, unpunished and undestroyed, standing in deliberate covenant contrast to the death that would follow unauthorized approach elsewhere in the Pentateuch. This meal, sealing the covenant just ratified through the blood of the sacrifice sprinkled on the people (Exo 24:8), foreshadows the greater covenant meal Christ would institute with His own disciples, the blood of the new testament, which is shed for many (Mat 26:28), fellowship with God made possible not by human worthiness but by blood applied.
webster_summary: Webster (1828), from CLEAR: bright; transparent; free of obscurity; the abstract noun here describing the sapphire-like pavement beneath God's feet, seen by Israel's elders at Sinai.
webster_full: CLEAR, adj. Bright; transparent; free from cloudiness or obscurity.
CLEARNESS, n. The quality or state of being clear; transparency; brightness.
In Exodus 24:10 the word describes the sapphire-like pavement beneath God's feet at Sinai.
The text describes only the pavement, not God's form, consistent with Scripture's caution against idolatry.
The vision is followed by a covenant meal: 'they saw God, and did eat and drink' (Exo 24:11).
scriptures: And they saw the God of Israel: and there was under his feet as it were a paved work of a sapphire stone, and as it were the body of heaven in his clearness.
corruption_summary: A curiosity that presses Scripture to visually describe God's own form, beyond what the text itself gives, misses the deliberate restraint the passage shows and the reason for it: an invisible God who forbids images made of Him.
corruption_paragraphs: Speculative interest can want more visual detail than the text supplies, but the passage's own restraint — describing only the pavement, never God's form — is itself theologically significant, consistent with the second commandment's prohibition against images of God (Exo 20:4).

This entry faces no significant postmodern redefinition. The principle to recover is the covenant meal that follows: fellowship with the holy God, made possible not by human worthiness but by the blood of the covenant just sprinkled (Exo 24:8), a pattern fulfilled in the blood of the new testament (Mat 26:28).
